lens: Voice read, last reader before publishing. Read-only. Text checked: /home/user/livewell-land/client/public/essays/the-children-rome-threw-away.json (title, excerpt as standfirst, Markdown body), read against /home/user/Livewell-/docs/work/essays/BRIEF.md, /home/user/Livewell-/docs/VOICE-JAMES-BELL.md, /home/user/Livewell-/docs/work/NOTES.md (biography) and the Forbidden Language list in /home/user/Livewell-/CLAUDE.md. I searched the list literally, then read the piece once as the skeptic and once as a pastor deciding whether to hand it to a congregation. I also compared it by 6-word overlap with the pilots, the drafts and the landed essays. Every old string below occurs exactly once (checked by script). All ten replacements were applied together to a scratch copy, and node scripts/validate-essays.mjs passes on it. The piece is strong and none of the findings restructures it. The three 'should' findings are the evenness of the abortion paragraph, who the pastoral section speaks to about abortion, and the recap at the head of the ending. Quotation wording and facts belong to the integrity lens. One note for that lens: the United States sentence in 'What the Church Did with Foundlings and Their Mothers' (Fessler) never says who ran the homes the women were sent to. A skeptic will ask what the church had to do with them. Any clause added to answer that needs a verified source, so I have not proposed one here.

findings.where: The Unwanted Child in Post-Christian America, paragraph 3, fourth sentence: "Others will speak up for the women and look away from the child."
findings.problem: The criticism fires in both directions but with two different instruments. The failure on the pro-life side gets a concrete scene the reader can see: "a pregnant seventeen-year-old in their own youth group." The other side gets one abstract clause about "the women." A reader on the right will feel the essay saved its specificity for him, and a reader on the left will feel let off. The brief asks for the same instrument and the same grief. The smallest fix puts the same girl in front of both groups and keeps the original verbs.
findings.fix: Replace "Others will speak up for the women and look away from the child." with: "Others will speak up for that same girl and look away from the child she is carrying."

findings.where: If You Have Lost a Child, paragraphs 1, 3 and 4: "And some of you have ended a pregnancy, and the lines from the Didache and Tertullian landed hard." / "If you ended a pregnancy, you are not a monster," / "Many churches and ministries quietly help women after an abortion,"
findings.problem: The essay's own thread is that men and institutions decided for women: "Hilarion decided for Alis what would happen if the baby was a girl. The homes decided for the mothers." Yet the pastoral section speaks about abortion only to the woman who ended a pregnancy. It never addresses the boyfriend, husband or parent who pressed for it or paid for it. The weight of the Didache line then falls on her alone, which is the pattern the section before it grieves. A pastor handing this to a congregation will think of the men in the pews. Three small insertions bring them into the address and into the mercy. (This finding does not overlap the separate fix to the end of the paragraph 3 sentence.)
findings.fix: Three replacements. (1) Replace "And some of you have ended a pregnancy, and the lines from the Didache and Tertullian landed hard." with: "And some of you have ended a pregnancy, or pressed someone else to end one, and the lines from the Didache and Tertullian landed hard." (2) Replace "If you ended a pregnancy, you are not a monster," with: "If you ended a pregnancy, or pushed someone toward it, you are not a monster," (3) Replace "Many churches and ministries quietly help women after an abortion," with: "Many churches and ministries quietly help women and men after an abortion,"

findings.where: Ending, first paragraph after the 988 paragraph: "The first Christians didn't end the abandonment of children in Rome, and the Christians who came after them didn't either. What they did was refuse it in their own houses, slowly and imperfectly, because they believed they had been taken in themselves. The church has forgotten that more than once since."
findings.problem: This paragraph is a recap. Its first sentence and the "slowly and imperfectly" clause restate how "Did the Early Christians Rescue Abandoned Babies?" ends ("Rescue came later and unevenly. Abandonment did not end when the empire became Christian, and Christians practiced it too.") before the mirror turn begins. "Slowly and imperfectly" also blurs the essay's own finding: the first Christians refused from their earliest documents, and it was rescue that came slowly. Keep the reason (they had been taken in) and the verdict (forgotten) and drop the summary, so the ending moves straight to the two questions.
findings.fix: Replace the whole paragraph "The first Christians didn't end the abandonment of children in Rome, and the Christians who came after them didn't either. What they did was refuse it in their own houses, slowly and imperfectly, because they believed they had been taken in themselves. The church has forgotten that more than once since." with: "The first Christians refused to put their children out because they believed they had been taken in themselves. The church has forgotten that more than once since."

findings.where: The Unwanted Child in Post-Christian America, paragraph 3, first sentence: "A church's politics can [blind it](/writing/the-conservative-blind-spot) to the parts of Scripture its side would rather not hear, and that is true [on the progressive side as well](/writing/the-progressive-blind-spot)."
findings.problem: The general claim links to the conservative essay, so the right reads as the default case and the left arrives as an afterthought ("as well"). It is small, but it makes the two sentences that follow feel unequal before they start. The fix keeps the same two links and targets and gives them equal weight.
findings.fix: Replace with: "A church's politics can blind it to the parts of Scripture its side would rather not hear, and that is as true [on the progressive side](/writing/the-progressive-blind-spot) as [on the conservative one](/writing/the-conservative-blind-spot)."

findings.where: Standfirst (excerpt), opening words: "In a world where leaving an unwanted newborn outside was an ordinary family decision,"
findings.problem: "In a world where" is a stock movie-trailer opener, the kind of standfirst template the judges flagged. Otherwise the sentence is one plain declarative sentence, not a balanced antithesis. Adding "Roman" also tells a reader on a listing page which world is meant.
findings.fix: Replace "In a world where leaving an unwanted newborn outside was an ordinary family decision," with: "When leaving an unwanted newborn outside was an ordinary Roman family decision,"

findings.where: If You Have Lost a Child, paragraph 3, end of first sentence: "you are not beyond the reach of the God this essay has been describing."
findings.problem: The most tender sentence in the piece steps outside itself to refer to "this essay." If a pastor reads it aloud to a woman who has had an abortion, the frame breaks at the worst moment. The God of Ezekiel 16 comes back in the closing lines anyway.
findings.fix: Replace "you are not beyond the reach of the God this essay has been describing." with: "you are not beyond the reach of God."

findings.where: The Unwanted Child in Post-Christian America, paragraph 2, last sentence: "It is after something both sides of it are tempted to leave undone."
findings.problem: This is a small announced turn. "Something" withholds what the essay is after, the next paragraph turns to blind spots, and the answer only arrives two paragraphs later. Name it.
findings.fix: Replace with: "It is after the care for mothers and children that both sides of it are tempted to leave undone."

findings.where: The Unwanted Child in Post-Christian America, paragraph 4, second sentence: "could tell her youth leader before she told anyone else, and be met with help"
findings.problem: "Before she told anyone else" reads as the church hearing the news ahead of her parents. Parents in the congregation will hear it that way, and a pastor will hesitate to hand the essay to them. The point is that she would not dread telling the church, not that the church comes first.
findings.fix: Replace with: "could tell her youth leader without dreading it, and be met with help"

findings.where: Why Roman Families Left Children Outside, paragraph 3, first sentence: "Few of us, with no wages yet and a wife at home with a small child, could be sure"
findings.problem: "A wife at home" quietly assumes a male reader, in an essay whose last section speaks to mothers. Naming Hilarion's place turns the line into a thought experiment any reader can enter, and the self-implication stays the same.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Few of us in Hilarion's place, with no wages yet and a wife at home with a small child, could be sure"

clean_checks: Forbidden Language, searched literally in the title, excerpt and body: zero hits for delve, leverage, unlock, transformative, navigate, tapestry, unpack, landscape, nuanced, multifaceted, authentic, journey and holistic. Zero hits for every phrase (in today's world, now more than ever, here's the thing, I want to be real with you, God's got this, gospel-centered, authentic community) and every therapy-speak item (hold space, your truth, do the work, your feelings are valid, lean into, showing up). 'foster' appears five times, all in the child-welfare term: foster care twice, foster parents three times. The forbidden sense is the verb, and scripts/lib/forbidden-language.mjs (ALLOWED) sets exactly these senses aside. There is no plain substitute for the legal name of the system, so no change. 'blessed' appears once, as a verb inside verbatim Scripture (Mark 10:16).
Em-dash: no U+2014 anywhere. The three en-dashes are all verse ranges (Ezekiel 16:5–6, and Psalm 68:5–6 in the body and in the Closing Texts).
Exclamation points: two, both "Live!" inside verbatim Ezekiel 16:6 with the reference beside it (the body quotation of 16:5–6 and the closing line).

Brief stamps: none of "Those of us who preach", "pastors like me", "This is not both-sidesism", "Consider ...", "none of this", "the record" or "I don't exempt myself". No "honest" or "fair" anywhere.

Rulebook leakage: none. No steelman, verdict, indictment or self-implication vocabulary. The fair hearing for the Romans is done without being announced ("most Romans were not cruel people, and Alis's position was a hard one").
Announced turns: none beyond finding 7. "Here the story usually told in churches runs ahead of the evidence" is the plain signposting the brief allows, and it is paid off at once.

Aphoristic closers and tidy triplets: no chiasmus, rhyme or epigram at paragraph ends worth cutting. The lists are real lists (the four-part sketch of Hilarion; what Christians who do better actually do; meals, babysitting, a night off). The last line's "to the child and to the mother, and to those of us who failed them both" names the essay's two subjects and then the reader, and it earns its three parts.

Internal repetition: the "Not X. Y." move comes about once per section, not once per paragraph. "Taken in" is the controlling image Scripture supplies (Ezekiel 16, Exodus 2, Galatians 4:5, Psalm 27:10) and is used as the voice standard asks, not stamped. "Monster" appears twice on purpose, once for Hilarion and once for the reader.

Scholar parade: the formula "In *Title* (YEAR), X argued" never appears. Three books are named, with no publication years. The densest stretch (Boswell, Harris, Engels, Stark) is a real dispute over numbers. Each name holds a distinct position, and Engels's argument carries the sex-ratio premise Stark depends on, so keep it.

Biography: none used. No title, years in ministry, book count, church name or Southern Baptist reference. The first person ("I don't know how to read these histories", "I don't want to hurry past any of that", "I've written elsewhere") is plain and is never used as a credential.

Headings: eight, all plain and descriptive (A Letter from Alexandria; Why Roman Families Left Children Outside; What the First Christians Taught; Why Christians Saw Children Differently; Did the Early Christians Rescue Abandoned Babies?; What the Church Did with Foundlings and Their Mothers; The Unwanted Child in Post-Christian America; If You Have Lost a Child).
Standfirst: one declarative sentence, not a balanced antithesis. Finding 5 deals only with its stock opener.

Political criticism fires in both directions. There is a conservative link and a progressive link, pregnancy centers sit beside prenatal care and paid leave, and the essay says "it tends to run along the same line our voting does." The historical criticism hits Catholic institutions (Italy, Tuam, Canada) and Protestant ones (Bethany Home; the Anglican, United and Salvation Army homes) with the same grief, and it refuses a Protestant reader any safe distance. Findings 1 and 4 even out the instrument.

Contested question: the law on abortion is named as dividing Americans and Christians alike and left open ("This essay won't settle that argument"). James's position on the law is not asserted. The moral teaching is given as the church's historic teaching, sourced to the Didache and Tertullian, and the pastoral section speaks of it as sin ("who carried sin like this to the cross"). That is the essay's one confessional claim on the subject. It is historic church teaching, not one of the second-order doctrines CLAUDE.md lists, so it is not flagged for James. It is noted here so the orchestrator knows it is there.

Ending: it leaves weight. Two real questions turn the mirror on "us" ("Would either of them be safe with us?") and it lands on Ezekiel 16:6 fulfilled in Christ and spoken to the child, the mother and "those of us who failed them both." There is no clever kicker. The one recap is finding 3.

Crisis path: present. [Find Help](/help) is linked, the 988 line is there word for word as the brief gives it, and the essay says it "can't give medical or counseling advice." Grief is honored and not hurried (Matthew 2:18, "he did not rebuke it"). No reader is diagnosed, despair is not validated, and forgiveness is offered through Romans 8:1 and Psalm 34:18. Abuse by a church leader is not in view in the present tense (the institutional harms are historical), so no reporting line is required. The crisis paragraph shares its wording with why-does-god-feel-far-away. That is standard safety wording, and the two essays do not link to each other.

Self-implication is done, not announced: "Few of us ... could be sure we would not have written the same sentence", "less heroic than we like to tell them", "It would be easy for a Protestant to read that and feel safely distant", "our voting", "safe with us", "those of us who failed them both".

Scripture is used as diagnosis inside the argument and read in context (Ezekiel 16 with "The rest of the chapter is a hard charge against the city's unfaithfulness"). Genesis 1:27, Mark 10, Matthew 18, Exodus 1–2, Galatians 4:5, Psalm 68, James 1:27, Matthew 2:18 and Romans 8:1 all do work. The Closing Texts lines are in the right *"Quote."* (Reference) format. Two of the three repeat verses from the body, as the approved pilots also do.

Links: three essay links (the-conservative-blind-spot, the-progressive-blind-spot, the-early-church-under-rome, all in link-targets.json) plus /help, inside the brief's two to four. The validator resolves all of them.

Register numbers: 3,786 words (inside the 2,500 to 3,800 range). The 44 body paragraphs average 83 words, mean sentence length is 18.6 words, and 16% of sentences run 8 words or fewer (below the pilots' quarter, which means fewer drumbeats, not a fault).

Reuse: 6-word overlaps with the pilots, the drafts and the landed essays come only from Scripture (Genesis 1:27, Psalm 34:18), the link anchor for the-early-church-under-rome, and the crisis line. No sentence or image is reused from a pilot.
Gate: node scripts/validate-essays.mjs on the published file is clean. The same gate on a scratch copy with all ten replacements above applied is also clean.
